13185 EFFICIENCY.md
# Cyrus v6: efficiency (cheaper mod generation, same quality)

Branch `feature/cyrus-v6-efficiency` (worktree `/tank/dev-worktrees/cyrus-v6-efficiency`). Service 0.5 patch to
`services/modbuilder/`, NOT deployed. Docs: DOCUMENTATION.md "AI Mod Builder: efficiency (service 0.5)".
Raw analysis output: `spend-2026-10-08.txt` (this folder).

## Method

- Read-only copy of the 138 `build.json` records on VM 88001 and the 4 Claude CLI session transcripts that
  still exist in the container (`tar` over ssh / `docker exec ... tar`; nothing on the VM was changed).
- `services/modbuilder/tools/spend.py` (new) over that copy. Prices: list prices (Sonnet 5 / 5.5 $2 in / $10 out,
  Haiku 4.5 $1/$5, Opus 5 $5/$25, Opus 5.5 $4/$20; cache read 0.1x input; cache write 1.25x (5 min) or 2x (1 h)).
- **No real builds were run (0 of the 6 allowed).** 0.5 can only run for real on VM 88001, which agents must not
  modify, and the AI credential must not be copied to node-2. Submitting builds to the live 0.4 service would not
  have measured anything new. So every "after" number below is an offline cost model, marked "est.".
- Quality gate offline: 29 unit / offline-pipeline tests (real `server.js`, fake CLI + javac), `tsc` clean. The
  real eval (`eval/run_eval.py v6`, ~$3) is the owner's step after deploy (install notes in the docs).

## Where the money goes today

Baseline = eval run v5 (the current default route, Sonnet 5.5, 30 builds, 28 succeeded, 0 repairs): **$0.098 / build**.

| Part | $ / build | Share | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| Output tokens | $0.060 | 61% | ~4.0k tokens of code that lands in files + ~2.4k other (thinking, text) |
| Cache writes | $0.033 | 33% | everything the model generated, written back to the cache at the **1 h TTL price (2x input)** |
| Cache reads | $0.006 | 6% | the ~15k-token cached prefix + history, re-read each request |
| Uncached input | ~0 | 0% | the prefix cache already works across builds |

Findings:
1. **Prompt caching already works.** First request of every build reads ~14.8k cached tokens (tools + system
   prompt + version sheet + rules); the system prompt is byte-identical per version. Nothing to gain there.
2. **The CLI writes the cache with the 1-hour TTL.** Only 2x pricing reproduces the reported cost (5 min model:
   $2.57 vs reported $2.94 for v5; 1 h: $2.94). That makes cache writes a third of the bill.
3. **Thinking is the biggest variable cost**: ~37-44% of Sonnet 5.5 output, ~71% on the Saka tier (Sonnet 5, avg
   $0.49 per fresh build, n=2, up to 31k thinking tokens in a single planning request), ~77% on Haiku. Thinking also
   gets written to and re-read from the cache during the tool loop, so it costs ~1.4x its output price.
4. **One file per request on the tiers**: the Saka and Katara transcripts wrote one file per API request (11 writing
   requests in one build), each re-reading the whole context. Sonnet 5.5 auto builds already batch (2-3 requests).
5. **Exploration turn**: a fresh build spent its first request on a `Glob` of the empty template folder (1 of the 2 fresh transcripts; the change-request transcript did the same before reading).
6. **Repairs are now rare** (2% of all spend; 0 in v5). Of the 13 historic builds that needed one, 7 failed only on
   mechanical things (final main class x2, import from the wrong package x2, Attribute prefix x3).
7. The Haiku "cheap first repair" really is cheap ($0.010-$0.021), even though switching model loses the cache
   (thinking is not carried across user turns, so the history it must re-cache is small, ~8k tokens).

## Savings table

| # | Lever | Status | Saving | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Saka tier -> Sonnet 5.5** (`MB_TIER_SAKA=claude-sonnet-5-5`, env only) | knob exists; **owner decision** | **~50% on Saka builds** (more on big ones) | measured: 0.3 eval, same 28 prompts, Sonnet 5 $0.203 -> 5.5 $0.104, first try 93% -> 100% |
| 2 | Effort (`MB_EFFORT=medium` for Sonnet/Opus; same value for every call of a build) | implemented, **off** | est. 15-20% if medium halves thinking | model: thinking ~$0.034 of $0.098 incl. its cache cost; unmeasured quality -> eval first |
| 3 | Cache TTL 5 min (`MB_CACHE_TTL=5m`) | implemented, **off** | est. 12% per build **only above ~15 builds/hour on the same version + model**; costs more below that | model: body cache writes 8.1k tokens x (2 - 1.25) x $2/M = $0.012; cold 15k prefix re-write $0.0375 at 5m vs $0.06 at 1h (Poisson break-even ~13-15/h) |
| 4 | Fresh builds: Read/Write/Edit only + "folder holds only the Gradle files" | implemented, **on** | est. 1-5% (a whole request when the model would have Globbed; ~1k fewer cached prefix tokens per request) | transcripts: first request was a Glob in 1 of the 2 fresh builds (the other read its reference image, as told); ~$0.005-0.007 each |
| 5 | Batching instructions (several Writes per response, never one per response; Reads together on changes; small Edits) | implemented, **on** | est. 0-3% on Sonnet 5.5 auto; 10-20% on Saka/Katara if followed | model: 11 single-file requests re-read ~300k cached tokens ($0.06) where 3 would read ~75k |
| 6 | Deterministic auto-fixes before a model repair (`autofix.js`) | implemented, **on** | est. 0-2% average; per affected build saves one repair ($0.01-$0.15) and 10-60 s | 7 of 13 historic repairs; also stops the pre-check's import rules spending a model turn (found by the offline pipeline test) |
| 7 | Repair turn cap 25 (`MB_MAX_TURNS_REPAIR`) | implemented, **on** | tail only | no repair in the records used > 8 |
| 8 | Exact-repeat reuse (`MB_DEDUPE=on`) | implemented, **off** | 100% of a repeated build | records: 15 repeats / 8% of spend, but those are eval re-runs, not customers; `dedupeKey` is now recorded on every build to measure the real rate |
| 9 | Yakko -> Opus 5.5 (`--build-arg CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION>=2.1.280`, `MB_TIER_YAKKO=claude-opus-5-5`) | Dockerfile arg added, **off** | est. 20% per token (list price) | Opus 5.5 defaults to effort medium: pin `MB_EFFORT` and eval before switching |

Combined, with only the default-on items (4-7): est. 2-8% on the default route, more on the tiers. The big money
is in decisions 1-3, which change model, effort or cache behaviour and so need the owner and/or the eval.

## Deliberately not done (protects quality, or does not pay)

- **Retrieving only the relevant cheat-sheet sections.** The whole sheet is ~4k tokens, cached, read at $0.20/M:
  about $0.002-$0.008 per build. Slicing it per request makes the prefix vary (more cache writes, which cost 20x
  a read), and a missed section is exactly the failure the sheets fixed (first try 89% -> 100% on 1.21.1). The
  research agent's CloudAPIBench note agrees: retrieval helps rare APIs, can hurt common ones. Keep it whole;
  revisit only for games whose packs are much bigger, and only with an eval.
- **Cheap planner + focused coder.** The planner's output does not remove the coder's own thinking, it adds a call
  with its own prefix, a wrong plan caps quality, and on the customer tiers it would change the model the customer
  chose. Effort (#2) is the same lever inside one model and one cache namespace.
- **A fresh, targeted repair session (only the failing file + error).** The resumed session already has the files
  in context and reads them from cache at 0.1x; a fresh session must write them to the cache again at 1.25-2x and
  loses the other files' context. Repairs are already targeted (errors + API lookup only, 8k cap).
- **Inlining the old source into change prompts.** Claude Code's Edit requires a prior Read of the file, so inlined
  files are read again anyway.
- **Changing effort or model per stage inside one build** (e.g. low effort for repairs): either invalidates the
  prompt cache; not worth it for a 1-2 request repair. The existing Haiku first repair stays (measured cheap).
- **Template library of building blocks the model composes.** Code in files is ~$0.04 per build; boilerplate is a
  fraction of that, and a library the model must learn (and that must be javap-verified per version and shaded
  per plugin) adds risk. Designed below as an eval experiment, not built.
- **Tool-output truncation.** Tool results here are tiny (Write acks, Glob lists); Reads on change requests are the
  files the model must see. Nothing to cut.
- **Lower generate turn cap.** Typical is 2-6 requests; the $2.50/call and $4/build budgets already bound the tail.

## Where the cost-versus-quality line sits (recommendation)

1. Take the free wins now: deploy 0.5 as is (items 4-7 on, everything else off) and run the v6 eval. Pass = 28/28,
   13/13 runtime, 2/2 refused, first try not below v5.
2. Move Saka to Sonnet 5.5. It was measured cheaper, faster and better; this is the single largest saving.
3. Then one bounded effort eval: v6 prompts at `MB_EFFORT=medium` vs default (about $3 per run, 2 runs). Adopt
   medium only if success, first try and runtime are unchanged; otherwise stay. Never go below medium for codegen.
4. Leave the cache TTL at the CLI default until traffic is above ~15 builds/hour per version + model; when the
   service moves from the subscription token to an API key, check the spend split again (the CLI's default TTL may
   differ) and pin `MB_CACHE_TTL=1h` while traffic is low.
5. Turn on `MB_DEDUPE` only after deciding what a reused build costs the customer (today it would be 0 tokens)
   and after `dedupeKey` shows real repeats (template chips are the likely source).

## For the economy agent (`lib/cyrus/estimate.ts`, `cyrus_tok_*`) - not changed here

The token charge is already the measured `costUsd`, so margins hold automatically; only the **estimates** drift:
- `BASE` usd ranges are anchored on Phase 0 Sonnet 5 ($0.28 avg). If Saka moves to Sonnet 5.5, change to roughly
  simple [0.05, 0.10], standard [0.08, 0.16], complex [0.15, 0.30] (eval 0.3: $0.066 / $0.102 / $0.189; v5
  complex max $0.24). If Saka stays on Sonnet 5, the current ranges fit (Saka measured $0.30 and $0.68).
- `costFactor`: katara 0.5 is low against Sonnet 5.5 (Haiku auto $0.066 vs 5.5 $0.098 = ~0.7); yakko 1.7 is low
  (one Opus 5 SimpleHeal cost $0.341, ~5x a simple Sonnet 5.5 build; n=1, so use ~3 until more data).
- Reserve table (`cyrus_tok_reserve_table`): same direction as `BASE`.
- With `MB_DEDUPE=on`, a reused build reports `costUsd` 0 and settles 0 tokens (`tokensForCost` returns 0 for 0).

## Knowledge packs: how the Minecraft sheets and rules map to GameSupport `knowledge`

`node services/modbuilder/tools/export-knowledge.js` prints them in the contract's shape now (1.21.1: 43 sheet
lines / 13 rules; 1.21.4: 42/15; 1.21.8: 42/16; 1.21.11: 42/17):
- `apiSheet` = one line per bullet of `sheets/<ver>.md`, prefixed by its section (`[Attributes] ...`), so a
  retriever can select by tag. The sheet stays generated by `gen-sheets.py` (javap-checked); do not hand-edit.
- `failureRules[]`: `id` <- id; `detect` <- `pattern` (source regex the pre-check runs) or `warning:<regex>` for
  rules that only show up as a compiler warning ("" = prompt-only lesson); `fix` <- `fix` (with `$1` capture
  placeholders) or `rule`; `why` <- `rule` + the build ids it was mined from (+ "main class only" for `scope`).
- Gaps in the contract worth adding: `knowledge` holds one `version`, but a game supports several (Minecraft: 4)
  -> make it `knowledge?: Pack[]` or a map by version; rules need `versions?: string[]` (one rule covers several),
  `scope?: "main"|"any"`, and `kind?: "source"|"compiler-warning"|"runtime"` instead of the `warning:` prefix;
  optional `autofix?: {replace: string}` for purely mechanical rules (what `autofix.js` does from the jar).
- Single source of truth: the build service runs JS inside its image and cannot import TS GameSupport. Keep each
  game's pack as JSON next to its build service (like `rules/failure-rules.json`) and have `lib/cyrus/games/<id>.ts`
  import or generate from it, rather than two copies.
- Retrieval: keep injecting the whole pack while it is a few thousand tokens (cached, see above). If a game's pack
  grows past ~10k tokens, select lines by section tag from the request + plan, put the selection AFTER the cached
  prefix (user turn), and gate it behind the eval.

## Template library (designed, not built)

Verified blocks (command executor + tab complete, config with reload, YAML data store, scheduler/cooldowns,
InventoryHolder menu, MiniMessage helper) in a fixed package `dev.nxeon.mb.lib`, pre-placed in the workspace and
listed (API only, ~500 tokens) in the cached system prompt. After the model finishes, the service deletes unused
blocks and relocates the used ones into the plugin's own package (no class clashes between plugins). Each block
javap-checked per version. Expected saving: part of the ~$0.04 code output on menu/data-heavy plugins. Ship only
if a v6-vs-blocks eval shows equal success, first try and runtime.

## Files and commits

`services/modbuilder/{server.js, usage.js (new), autofix.js (new), prompts.js, precheck.js, run.sh, Dockerfile,
tools/spend.py (new), tools/export-knowledge.js (new)}`, `test/modbuilder-efficiency.test.ts`,
`test/modbuilder-pipeline.test.ts`, `docs/DOCUMENTATION.md`.

content.thinking:
By default, guard refusals charge full cost with a 5-token floor, so "refunds for guard refusals" isn't quite accurate -- it's really that settlement only returns the held amount, not that refusals are refunded.

I should recommend making false refusals free while keeping the 5-token charge as abuse deterrence for legitimate refusals.

Looking at the settle/charge logic, charge is computed as tokensForCost(costUsd) × multiplier (1.25 for Yakko), and this includes the guard Haiku cost plus all repairs. That means users pay for repairs even when caused by our own failures or autofix issues, while only builds that fail entirely on our side get the free-with-3-per-week treatment -- a successful build with multiple repair rounds is fully charged to the user despite the plan screen's cost estimates not accounting for that variance. content.thinking:
Imports account for about 12.8% of characters and are strictly mechanical, so that portion could be auto-generated or fixed with existing import-correction tooling rather than hand-written.

That said, the dollar savings would be small—roughly 450 output tokens per build, less than $0.005—since autofix can already add missing imports deterministically. Code tokens are a minority of total cost anyway, so I'm now modeling the full cost breakdown per build (output tokens for code vs. text, plus cache writes) using actual measured numbers from a Sonnet build to see where the real savings opportunities lie.

Adding up the realistic scaffold-achievable savings across lifecycle, config loading, persistence, imports, and command skeletons, I land around 33% of code tokens saved, which translates to roughly 12-20% of total output tokens. In dollar terms that's about $0.013-0.04 per build (3-8% savings), and accounting for the cache-write multiplier on those output tokens, the effective savings factor increases by about 1.4x.

But that's a modest lever compared to a bigger one: shifting designer lanes from writing full code to writing compact JSON specs, which could cut thousands of code tokens down to a few hundred. Still, actual measured designer-lane build costs aren't cheap -- one build hit $0.43 plus $0.21 for asset repair, with 26 turns and 29 files touched, so I need to dig into the flight JSON logs to compare designer-lane costs against plain builds directly.

// Cyrus R3 gameplay designers: the DESIGN IR. A typed Custom Item Designer spec (ItemDesign) with an ability/event
// graph (AbilityGraph = trigger -> conditions -> actions, with branches) that the compiler (./compile.ts) turns into
// straight Java calling the verified component library (./components). Nothing here is free-form code: every node is a
// fixed kind, every number has a hard min/max (CAPS below; the JSON Schema carries them too), every activation has a
// static worst-case resource budget that must fit BUDGET, loops are bounded (query_* `max`, delayed `delayTicks` and
// nesting depth) and there is no way to run a command or arbitrary code. Numbers, texts and sound keys become config.yml
// parameters (editable without regenerating the mod, see ./params.ts); structure (kinds, effects, particles, targets)
// is code.
//
// Files: the build model writes one ItemDesign per file at assets/designs/<id>.json; a mod has at most
// DESIGN_LIMITS.maxItems of them. Identifiers live in the project's reserved namespace (engine-core identifiers):
// an item's full id is `nx_<8>:<id>`. Validation never throws: { ok, design | errors, warnings, checks, budgets }.
// The JSON Schema (designer.v1.schema.json) is generated from these Zod types (scripts/cyrus/build-designer-artifacts.ts;
// a test fails while it is stale).
import { z } from "zod";
import { NAMESPACE_RE, buildIdentifier } from "../engine-core/identifiers";
import { IngredientSchema, TEXT_COLORS, canonicalJson } from "../datapack/spec";
import { compareMc, isVanilla, missingIdReason, vanillaIds } from "../datapack/versions";
import { getVersion } from "../versions/registry";

export const DESIGN_SPEC_VERSION = 1;
export { canonicalJson };

/** Per-mod limits. */
export const DESIGN_LIMITS = { maxItems: 6, maxSpecBytes: 64 * 1024, maxAbilities: 6, maxNodes: 48, maxDepth: 3, maxConditions: 8, maxActions: 16, maxMarks: 4, maxPassives: 4, maxLore: 6, maxPermissions: 8 } as const;

/**
 * Hard caps on every number (inclusive). The config loader clamps to the SAME caps at runtime, so a hand-edited
 * config.yml can never exceed them. Ticks: 20 = 1 second.

content.thinking:
I'm cataloging the existing spec kinds — item abilities, menus, quests, bosses, datapack elements, worldgen, config, creatures, sound, texture — and sorting which archetypes could be made fully spec-driven with no free-form code needed.

I'm grouping archetypes into tiers: those already fully expressible through datapack/designer lanes (recipes, loot, enchantments, fishing, advancements, worldgen, menus, shops, quests, projectiles, food, weapons, bosses, HUD elements), those needing spec plus a thin layer of glue code (warps, NPCs, skills, leaderboards, rewards, cutscenes, potions, music), and those that remain mostly pure code but could still be templated.

That last category covers simple CRUD-style command/data plugins -- homes, tpa, rtp, warps, kits, announcer, chat features, join/leave, afk, books, signs, heads, holograms, vanish -- which look like strong candidates for a new parameterized "rule/behavior" spec type. Then there's a final tier of systems that genuinely require custom code: claims, regions, minigames, clans, economy, auction, machines, mob AI, structure placement. I'm now trying to tally the 85 rows into these buckets, starting with the "spec-driven today" group where the model only needs to write spec JSON and Java compiles with zero extra tokens -- recipes, loot, enchantments, fishing, advancements, worldgen, menus, shops, quests, projectiles, food, weapons, bosses, various HUD specs, music, creature specs, and partially cutscenes and NPCs.

Rather than relying purely on judgment, I think it's better to pull the "technique.cyrus" field directly from the data for each archetype, since it already labels whether something is "plain plugin with sheets/golden reference" versus "designer item" etc. -- that gives a more objective categorization than guessing lane assignments myself.

Looking at the numbers: 18 of 85 archetypes are primarily spec-lane driven, while 63 are plain/plugin archetypes with 54 having a golden reference. Golden references average around 60 lines, much shorter than real customer prompts which run 100-1600 characters, so I want to inventory what overhead the Claude CLI itself adds through tool definitions and system pieces.

The first request of each build reads roughly 14.8k cached tokens covering tools, system prompt, version sheet, and rules. With the system prompt base around 10.05k tokens plus tool definitions, total runs about 13-14k baseline, climbing to 28k with all feature lanes active. At Sonnet's cache-read pricing of $0.20/M, ten turns reading 14k tokens costs about $0.028, which is trivial, but cold cache writes are the real cost driver -- since the system prompt varies by version and lane combination, most low-traffic builds pay a cold write of 14-28k tokens, running $0.056-0.11 on Sonnet but up to $0.28 on Opus for a fully-laned prompt. That's a meaningful fixed cost at low traffic, compounded by the CLI's 1-hour cache TTL requiring a 2x write multiplier versus 1.25x for a 5-minute TTL, which only pays off above roughly 15 builds per hour per prefix.

Switching to a 5-minute TTL would save about 37.5% on cold prefix write costs when there's no cross-build reuse, since hits only land within that narrower window versus the full hour -- though at a few bursty builds per hour, the 1-hour window might still win on reads, so it's genuinely unclear without real data. To quantify this I'd need per-call token breakdowns, which aren't stored unless CYRUS_LEARNING is enabled, so a quick, code-free first step would be flipping that env knob on to start capturing the numbers. Separately, I'm noting that the Haiku guard calls show a clear cache effect, dropping from $0.015 on a cold first call down to $0.001-0.009 once warm.

Now I'm building out the full spend inventory, starting with the planner's Haiku call -- roughly $0.001-0.004 per plan-screen request, cached for 10 minutes per text and absorbed by Nxeon rather than billed to a build record, triggered any time new text comes in since the route doesn't pass the `needs` flag to control recomputation.

Then I'm tallying the guard call (one per build, $0.001-0.009, averaging $0.0043 across 18 measured calls, charged to the user with a 5-token minimum floor even on refusal), confirming the classifier is skipped entirely since the guard's tier override replaces it, and moving into generate (roughly 50% of total spend), change builds, and repairs. Repairs run cheap Haiku first then fall back to Sonnet, costing $0.222 across 7 calls (3% of spend), with repair-asset calls being pricier per turn at $0.215 over just 2 calls.

I'm noting that autofix, precheck/perfcheck/scan, and compile are all deterministic or compute-only steps with no model cost, running on the Nxeon VM, while title/description/tagline/summary/howToUse generation is handled by the main model.

I'm tracing whether listing category auto-sort is deterministic by checking for any model call in the autoSort logic, and separately flagging that asset generation (textures, sounds, creature specs) is mostly deterministic rendering from model-written spec JSON with no extra calls -- except the sound library catalog, which at 22.8KB (~5.7k tokens) gets read into context when enabled, adding a notable chunk of cached-write and per-turn-read cost on top of the ~1.5k token sound section already in the system prompt.

I'm estimating that catalog read cost at roughly $0.03 per build, worth 5-10% of a typical build's total, and thinking slicing the catalog by category or keyword retrieval would cut that down significantly -- I want to check how sounds.js places the catalog and whether the model truly has to read the whole thing.

I'm also running through the remaining pieces: MCP catalog tools are off, config studio adds a modest fixed token cost, reference images cost roughly 1.5k tokens each based on size, dedupe is off, and the new prompt-coach branch (an optional Haiku rewrite) isn't merged yet so its cost attribution is still unclear. I'm noting the weekly learning/mining job is deterministic and compute-only, the in-game AI gateway is just a stub, interrupted or unavailable builds carry no cost, and I still need to check the library ingest stage for its offline Nxeon-side model cost.

Imports are heavy since they involve reading user code with real token cost, while designer edit builds and config-only repacks are free. Now I'm digging into the hidden costs users silently absorb: the guard's token floor causing false refusals still gets charged, repairs on otherwise successful builds are fully charged without the user being able to anticipate it, cold-cache prefix writes add a fixed but invisible system-prompt cost not reflected in the lane estimate, and change/rework builds re-reading the workspace add further charges. I'm also noting the free-failure allowance -- three free timeouts per seven days before failures get charged in full -- plus that cancelled or interrupted builds can still be marked as chargeable depending on the flag.

I'm also tracking the Opus multiplier adding a 25% premium on top of its already 2.5x raw per-token cost versus Sonnet, and that escalations after two failed repairs silently bump the model tier (Katara to Saka to Yakko) and charge the user at the higher tier's rate without asking, even though the cost calculation still references the original model's multiplier for its base. Holds exceeding actual charges get refunded fine, and there's a flat 5-token minimum spend floor regardless of actual usage.

Comparing the plan screen's estimated cost ranges against real build costs, I'm seeing actual charges exceed the upper bound of the estimated range in multiple cases -- builds estimated to cost $0.30-0.60 or $0.15-0.35 ending up actually costing $0.68-0.82, showing the estimator consistently undershoots real usage for complex prompts.

content.thinking:
I need to flag a caveat here: since the Saka tier actually ran on claude-sonnet-5 while my cost estimates were anchored on Phase 0 Sonnet pricing with tiny eval prompts, the real token charges will likely run about 2.4-2.5x higher than what the plan screen displayed, at least until Saka transitions over.

There's also a deeper honesty issue in how the hold is computed — the hold range gets raised to the estimate plus 20%, but actual charges aren't capped at that reserve, so users can see "overHeld" amounts that exceed what the plan screen led them to expect. I want to propose showing calibrated "typically X, up to Y" ranges based on recorded p50/p90 stats per tier and lane combination instead.

Separately, I'm trying to figure out what share of total spend is actually model-generated code versus pre-made structures, since the v6 note dismissed template libraries as negligible. Without direct token counts, I'm estimating token usage from cost and duration data for real builds like mb907 to get a rough breakdown.

I'm working through the cost math — output tokens, cache writes, cache reads — to reverse-engineer how much of the spend is visible output versus thinking tokens, landing on something like 60-75% being thinking/planning rather than final code. This matches an owner's observation that planning time dominates wall-clock duration, with 3-4 minutes of thinking before the first tool call on a modest spec. That points to effort routing and thinking budget as the biggest lever, especially since the CLI defaults to high effort for Sonnet/Opus unless explicitly overridden.

I'm proposing effort should be chosen once per build based on guard complexity and recipe-hit status (so caching isn't broken by mid-build changes), with simple/recipe-hit builds dropping to low/medium effort — potentially saving 20-40% of build cost if thinking drops proportionally. I'm also considering whether MAX_THINKING_TOKENS could serve as a budget cap alternative to --effort, though on newer adaptive-thinking models it may only be respected when set to zero.

Now I'm sketching a deterministic scaffold that avoids redundant model work: since the model already writes modbuilder.json with command/permission declarations, I could generate plugin.yml automatically from that manifest instead of having the model duplicate the same information across two files.

This duplication is avoidable too — config.yml comments could be parsed to derive the config array in modbuilder.json automatically, eliminating another redundant pass. Together these fixes save roughly 1-2% of a typical build's output tokens, a small but safe win since the service would simply be deriving one artifact from another rather than trusting model-written duplication.

For the main class skeleton, I'm thinking of a JavaPlugin structure with onEnable handling default config, command/listener registration, and initialization, plus onDisable for cleanup. I'd also pre-place a reusable NxKit helper library offering typed config accessors with clamping, MiniMessage-based messaging, debounced async per-player data storage, a declarative command registry with permission/argument/tab-complete support, cooldown helpers, a paginated menu builder, and timing utilities — documented in the system prompt as a cached API reference so plugins can lean on shared infrastructure instead of reinventing it each build.

Estimating the actual savings, boilerplate categories like imports, lifecycle methods, config loading, persistence, and command dispatch skeletons add up to roughly 37% of code characters, and the scaffold could cut that down to maybe 25-30% net savings in code tokens -- translating to only about 8-12% output savings and 5-8% total cost savings per build, since code is just one portion of total tokens. There's also a risk the model misuses the helper APIs and triggers compile repairs, so I'd need to verify the helper's API surface is stable and version-tested across the four target Paper API versions. Overall this scaffold approach seems like a modest 5-10% lever compared to bigger wins like effort routing or using Sonnet with better recipes, which could yield 20-40%.

A bigger version of the idea would extend the designer lane's spec-driven approach (currently used for items, menus, quests, bosses, HUD) to cover more gameplay archetypes as parameterized templates, which could cut code output by 70-90% for those cases since the model fills a compact JSON spec instead of writing full code -- but I'm realizing the designer lane's system prompt sections (design, gameplay, boss, HUD, motion) already add up to around 8k tokens, which eats into any savings and isn't yet proven out by actual production cost data.

I don't have solid measured costs for designer-lane builds across these archetypes, so I should flag that this needs a proper eval rather than assuming savings. I'm also thinking through the cache fragmentation problem: since the system prompt differs per lane combination, version, and model, every unique combo creates its own cache prefix, so with low traffic the cache hit rate on anything but a single user's repeated builds is essentially zero.

So right now every build pays the full cold-write cost. For Sonnet with tools plus base prompt plus lane sections, that cold prefix write alone eats roughly 12-15% of a typical build's total cost. The fix is to reorder the prompt so the stable, version-dependent bulk (rules, sheet, perf) forms a shared prefix across all lane combinations, with lane-specific sections appended last -- though I need to check whether the toolset itself (fresh vs full) sits before or after that shared block, since that also breaks the prefix match.

But fresh vs change builds use different tool arrays, so they'd never share a cache prefix even with reordering, and the same applies across models since Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus never share. That gives version × tools × model = 24 distinct prefix variants, and since the CLI likely sends the system prompt as one single block with one cache_control breakpoint at the end, any variation anywhere in that text results in a total cache miss rather than a partial hit -- unless there's a way to place an earlier breakpoint, like on the tools array itself.

One fix would be moving the lane-specific sections out of the system prompt and into the first user message, keeping the system prompt identical for a given version/model/toolset combination so its cache entry stays warm across many lane variants, even though the lane content itself still gets written fresh each time as part of the user turn.

The savings from a warm hit work out to roughly $0.0475 per Sonnet build, $0.12 for Opus, $0.024 for Haiku — but how often that warmth actually happens depends heavily on traffic patterns, which are currently sparse but would tighten up a lot under heavier usage. A scheduled keep-warm ping to force cache hits isn't worth the cost though.

I'm also weighing the cold-write side: the 6.2k-token sheet portion of the system prompt costs about $0.025 per cold Sonnet build and $0.062 for Opus just to write into cache, so slicing that sheet down could cut cold-build costs even though it risks hurting cache reuse elsewhere.

Server owners change numbers in a settings editor, not by asking you, so EVERY tunable value is a setting: health, speed, damage, attack speed, knockback, cooldowns, durations, ranges, chances, counts, prices, rewards, spawn rules, timers, messages, sounds, colours, on/off switches. {"schemaVersion":1,"reload":{"command":"/<your command> reload"},"groups":[{"id":"stats","label":"Stats"}],"params":[{"key":"mobs.frost_zombie.max_health","group":"stats","type":"number","label":"Max health","help":"one short line","default":40,"unit":"hp","min":1,"max":1024,"safe":{"min":4,"max":200},"applies":"reload"}],"presets":[{"id":"hard","label":"Hard","values":{"mobs.frost_zombie.max_health":80}}]}
- type: number | int | duration (with "durationUnit": "ticks" | "s" | "ms") | range ([low, high]) | bool | enum ("options":[{"value":"auto"}]) | text ("maxLength") | color ("#rrggbb") | sound-ref (namespaced key) | list ("item":{"type":"text"}) | table ("columns":[{"key":"item","label":"Item","type":"text"},{"key":"chance","label":"Chance","type":"number","min":0,"max":1}]).
- min/max are hard limits (your code must never break inside them); "safe" is the balanced range (optional). key = the exact config.yml path. label max 60 characters, help max 200.
- "applies": "reload" when your reload subcommand re-reads it (then declare "reload" and register that command in plugin.yml), "restart" when it is only read at startup (spawn rules, registered recipes), "live" only when the code re-reads it on its own.
- "visual" (optional) links a stat to the preview: {"channel":"clipRate","clip":"walk","ref":0.23} for movement speed, "attackRate" for attack speed, "scale" for size, "fireRate" for a gun's rounds per minute.
- Start from the template keys given in the request (rename the section to fit your mod, drop what does not apply, add what your mod needs).
- READ every declared key in the code with getConfig().getDouble/getInt/getLong/getBoolean/getString/getStringList/getMapList("<exact key>") (or read a section with getConfigurationSection and then the key). A declared key the code never reads fails the build. Never hard-code a number that has a setting. Reload: reloadConfig() and re-read every value (re-apply stats to entities that already exist where it matters).
- Nxeon writes config.yml FROM the schema (commented, with units and limits); you may still write src/main/resources/config.yml, but the schema's defaults win. In modbuilder.json "config" may stay empty (Nxeon lists the settings).`;

content.thinking:
For the recipes design, I'm figuring out how to hook into existing mechanisms: the planner lanes in decide.ts, the assets.plan array, learning export records, and the golden harness. I'm thinking through how a recipe hit could flow through the planBlock injection and into the build service alongside the rest of the plan.

For retrieval, I'm leaning toward deterministic archetype matching via keyword/trigram index over the coverage JSON, and realizing the guard Haiku call could piggyback archetype ids onto its existing output with almost no extra token cost. For the path memory table, I'm sketching archetype/lane/tier combinations mapped to success rates and cost percentiles built from weekly BuildSignals, but with only 27 builds so far I'd need Bayesian shrinkage toward the base priors until there's enough effective sample size.

Now I'm defining the recipe schema itself — id, archetype ids, applicable versions, config params, API facts, pitfall links, a skeleton template or reference snippet, RCON test expectations, provenance tracking (author, sources, review status), and cost stats, with a draft/verified/retired status flag. For injection, I'm thinking a few hundred tokens of pattern guidance plus pitfalls and config keys, with only small skeleton snippets (30-60 lines) for genuinely tricky parts like async chunk-loading, since the 54 existing golden archetypes already provide reference source material for most of these patterns.

Converting those goldens into recipes costs roughly $0.005-0.02 per injection, and break-even math suggests this pays off if it saves even 700 output tokens of thinking or repair work — which seems very likely since a recipe skeleton replaces a lot of design thinking. The bigger win is quality: fewer pitfalls means fewer repairs. I estimate a recipe hit could cut thinking by 15-30%, avoid a chunk of the repair spend (which is a disproportionately expensive 23% of rework despite being only 6% of total spend), and save some code tokens via the skeleton — altogether maybe 15-35% savings on a hit, with hit rates of 40-60% for typical plugin requests given the 54 goldens already covering top archetypes.

So overall this could save 6-20% of total spend, but I need to validate with A/B testing using the existing coverage eval sets. The golden harness's RCON-based tests can double as the recipe test suite directly. For legal safety, I want a mandatory provenance field and a CI gate that checks recipe text for n-gram overlap against the private reference-mod corpus and other user builds, ensuring nothing derived copies code verbatim — recipes must be described in our own words, with authorship and lineage tracked per recipe.

For the learning pipeline, I'm designing it to mine only anonymized outcome records (counts, metadata, failure-rule ids, archetype ids) — never raw text or code — and have a weekly job surface "path-memory" and recipe-candidate suggestions for human review before any recipe version changes. Success is defined as completed, kept, under median cost, with no rework, and fixes are tracked by mapping failure signatures to what resolved them, all derived strictly from error codes and symbols rather than user code itself.

Now I'm thinking about recipe invalidation when Paper versions bump — recipes get tagged with version + sheet hash, triggering golden re-tests on any version addition. On the plan screen, I want token estimates shown as honest calibrated ranges (p50–p90) by tier and lane, falling back to a prior × correction factor when sample size is small, with chips like "uses a tested pattern" only showing quantified savings when there's enough data (n≥8), and I'm clarifying that charges settle to actual usage rather than being capped at the reserved hold.

I'm flagging a possible policy where charges could be capped at hold×1.0 with the system absorbing overages, pending an owner decision. I'm also finding that the change-cost factor of 0.8× doesn't hold uniformly — Saka's change/fresh ratio is close to 0.8 but both exceed estimates by 2.4x, while Katara's ratio is actually 1.7x higher since it explores more, suggesting per-tier factors are needed instead of one flat multiplier.

Now I'm moving into ranking savings levers by (saving × confidence)/(effort & risk), using the 28-build sample to compute baseline stats — average cost per success around $0.27, with Katara at $0.12, Saka at $0.39, and Yakko at $0.37, where Saka accounts for 47% of total spend — before building out the full lever list with estimated savings ranges.

I'm referencing existing levers already covered elsewhere (effort routing, regression guards, multi-edit, repair caps, route floors, smaller sheets) without repeating them, then introducing new numbered levers: effort routing by guard class potentially saving 8-20% of total spend with medium-low confidence, a calibrated plan-screen estimate fix for trust rather than token savings, and a proposal to pre-seed or strip generated runtime files from the change workspace with a file manifest.

I'm estimating that skipping reads of generated code (NxPerf, designer runtime) could save 6-13% of spend if 15-30% of change-build costs come from avoidable reads, but checking real data complicates this: comparing an actual change build ($0.427, 17 turns) against a fresh build of similar size ($0.676, 9 turns) suggests the cost is dominated by output/thinking turns rather than context reads, since per-turn overhead from cached reads is small.

Turn count seems more tied to model behavior (Sonnet 5 vs 5.5) than to file-reading patterns, so I'll keep this as a low-confidence but cheap-to-fix issue — adding a "generated, do not read" manifest makes sense especially for larger designer runtime files. I'm also sizing up how much of the code is boilerplate: across sampled decompiled files, imports, lifecycle, config-loading, persistence, and skeleton code add up to roughly 38% of code characters, which translates to around 23% of code tokens when scaled realistically — and since visible code is maybe a quarter to two-fifths of total output, and output drives most of the cost, this boilerplate share could meaningfully affect spend.

Running the numbers on actual builds, code tokens look like they account for anywhere from 15% to 40% of per-build cost depending on complexity, so if scaffolding removes about 23% of that code, it saves roughly 4-10% of cost per fresh build overall, with additional savings possible from import elision and config dedup. This ranks below effort routing and recipe templates in priority, though it synergizes well with recipes since recipe skeletons would call into the scaffold. My honest takeaway for the owner is that pre-made structures save modestly—around 5-10%—because most tokens go toward thinking and cached context rather than the code itself, so the real value of structure comes from replacing code with typed specs.

Looking at designer-lane expansion as a next tier: about 18 of 85 archetypes are currently spec-driven, and roughly 25 of 63 plain archetypes follow a CRUD/command/message/schedule pattern (custom commands, kits, homes/warps, join/leave messages, announcers, chat formatting) that a typed "commandKit" spec could cover for 60-80% of requests, cutting tokens by 50-80% and eliminating compile errors since the compilation would be deterministic. The tradeoff is that building this would require an XL effort (IR design, compiler, simulator, tests) and carries expressiveness risk, meaning it'd need a hybrid fallback to free-form code when the spec can't capture something.

To validate the hit rate, I want to check how many of the 25 fresh/lineage root build prompts actually fit these candidate archetypes (teleport family, kits, message family, cooldown commands), estimating savings per build of roughly $0.15-0.4 on Sonnet-5 or $0.05-0.1 on 5.5. # BL: Cyrus token-savings plan (2026-10-12)

Owner goal: if a simple mod costs people too many tokens, Cyrus is not worth it. This note finds every place tokens or compute are spent, measures what can be measured, and ranks the ways to cut spend without making mods worse. It extends BJ (token baseline) and BK (learning loop); BJ's levers are listed in the ranking by number but not re-analysed. Companion: `BL-recipe-memory-design.md`.

Labels: **V** = verified in code (cyrus-rc2) or in read-only SELECTs of the production `ModBuild` table / decompiled jars of the 25 stored builds. **U** = estimate or judgment, with the assumption stated. No build was run, nothing was written anywhere except these two files.

**Sample warning (V):** production holds 28 builds, ALL from the owner (1 distinct user), $7.33 total. Nothing here is a forecast for public traffic. The numbers rank where to look and what to measure.

---

## 0. The five findings that matter

1. **Where the money is (V + U).** Code the model writes is only about 25-40% of a build's cost (U). The rest is thinking before the first edit (planning = 51% of wall time, BJ; the owner saw 3.5-4 min on a 700-word spec), one API round trip per file on Sonnet 5, and cold prompt-cache writes. Shrinking prompts, sheets or boilerplate is therefore worth single digits; model choice, effort, turn count and rework are worth tens of percent.
2. **The Saka tier is on Sonnet 5, not 5.5 (V).** All 12 Saka calls in the data resolved to `claude-sonnet-5` (`MB_TIER_SAKA` default). A fresh Saka build: median $0.55 (range $0.22-0.83), 9-10 turns, 450 s. The 0.3 eval measured Sonnet 5.5 at 2-3 requests and 49% cheaper. This is the largest single lever (BJ #1) and needs no code.
3. **The plan screen under-states cost (V).** I ran the real `estimate()` over the 25 successful builds: **20 exceeded the top of the shown range**, 3 were inside, 2 under. Median actual / shown-high: Saka fresh 2.4x, Saka change 2.5x, Katara change 2.1x, Katara fresh 1.0x, Yakko 1.2x. Users are charged actual cost (not capped at the hold), so the plan screen is the biggest "silently more expensive than shown" problem. See section 3.
4. **Owner's pre-made-structures idea: real but modest on tokens (V shares, U savings).** Of the code the model writes, about 26% is scaffoldable boilerplate (section 4), which is 4-10% of a plain build's cost. Its bigger value is removing failure classes (plugin.yml/getCommand mismatch, unsaved data, reload) and feeding recipes. Typed specs that compile to Java (designer lanes) save far more per hit (70-90% of code tokens) but only 18 of 85 archetypes use them today.
5. **Two things that look like savings are traps (V).** `MB_DEDUPE=on` is cross-user (the key has no user id): it would hand one customer another customer's source, which breaks the owner's "never reproduce a user's mod" rule. And "refunds for guard refusals" only release the hold: `cyrus_tok_charge_refused` defaults to true, so a refused or falsely refused request still costs the 5-token floor.

### Silently paid by the user (flag these)

1. **Cold-cache prefix writes and thinking** (rows 9-10): the biggest terms, not visible, not in the estimate.
2. **Repairs and asset repairs on a SUCCESSFUL build** (rows 6-8): fully charged (the failure-credit rule `cyrus_tok_free_failures=3` per 7 days applies to FAILED builds only; over the limit failures are charged in full). The 10-12 Spawner-Wand build spent 33% of its $0.65 on two asset-repair rounds.
3. **Escalation** (row 7): a Katara build can be finished by Sonnet or Opus without telling the user.
4. **The guard** (row 2): charged even when it refuses, including false refusals (the 10-12 06:52 ChunkMirror refusal charged 5 tokens, 215 returned). `cyrus_tok_charge_refused` is a Setting.
5. **Charge is not capped at the hold** (`settleCharge` charges full `costUsd`; the ledger only caps at the balance). With estimates 2.4x low, most builds end "over held". The UI shows it, but the user never agreed to it.
6. **Rework** (BJ: 23% of spend re-requested within 30 min), a share of which is the product's fault (planner turned "mob spawner" into a Spawner Wand and replaced the plugin).
7. **Per-build worst case**: `MB_BUILD_BUDGET_USD=4` and `MB_CALL_BUDGET_USD=2.5` default; the largest observed build is $0.83. A runaway loop could charge 2,000 tokens (40% of a daily cap of 5,000) before it stops.

Not charged to users: planner, coach, Test Flight, javac/scan compute, learning jobs, evals.

## 4. Owner's idea: pre-made structures (measured)

### 4.1 How much of a real build is boilerplate (V shares, U savings)

Method: decompiled (Vineflower) the 25 stored jars, kept only classes the MODEL wrote (excluded the injected `nxperf/` watchdog, 1,009 lines per build, and compiled `designer/`, `abilities/`, `items/`), classified every line by method role. 15 builds, 55 files, 5,840 lines, about 56k tokens (chars/3.5). Our 65 golden plugins (hand-authored reference source, 4,213 lines) for comparison.

| category | real builds (chars) | golden (chars) | scaffold-addressable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| imports + package | 12.8% | 23.4% | yes: API imports can be resolved by the service (autofix already knows the unique FQN); JDK ones stay |
| lifecycle (onEnable/onDisable) | 5.3% | 7.5% | mostly (registration, timers, flush) |
| config loader / clamp / reload | 4.3% | 0 | yes (typed `Cfg` + generated config.yml) |
| persistence (YAML load/save) | 2.6% | 0.8% | yes (`Store`) |
| command dispatch skeleton (onCommand/onTabComplete) | 11.4% | 28.9% | about half: sender/perm/args/usage checks |
| fields, structure, annotations, small helpers | 7.9% | 11.5% | partly |
| **event handlers** | 13.4% | 12.4% | no (skeleton line only) |
| **unique logic** | 41.2% | 15.4% | no |

Realistic saving: imports -80% (10.2 pts), lifecycle -70% (3.7), config -70% plus config-backed fields (5), persistence -70% (1.8), commands -55% (6.3), rest -30% (1.2) = **about 26% of code tokens** (range 20-30%).

Code is 15-40% of a build's cost (ChunkDup 15%, eval-size mods up to 41%; U), so a scaffold saves **4-10% of a fresh plain build** (U). Extra, smaller wins from the same family: derive `plugin.yml` from registered commands (median 576 chars = 170 tokens, V from the jars), `modbuilder.json` commands/permissions/config lists (duplicate of yml; ~200-500 tokens), and `config.yml` vs Config Studio's `schema.json` (both written; schema is the source) = 1-3%.

Where a scaffold also pays: it deletes failure classes the repair loop pays for today (getCommand without a yml entry, no flush in onDisable, no reload, unbounded queue), and is the host for recipes. Same injection mechanism as NxPerf (V: `perf.js inject`, 790 + 219 lines placed before every javac), so there is precedent and a safe pattern.

Verdict: build it, but behind recipes and effort routing in the order (it is an L-size item for single-digit percent). Do not expect it to fix the thinking cost.

### 4.2 Spec-driven archetypes (designer lanes and datapack lanes)

`lib/cyrus/adapters/minecraft-coverage.json`, 85 archetypes (V counts): 63 are "plain plugin / plugin" (54 have a golden), 18 are driven by a typed lane (menus_gui, bossbar_titles, hud_glyphs, sidebar, custom_music, advancements, armor_sets, custom_enchantments, custom_food, custom_weapons, loot, recipes, retexture_vanilla, custom_blocks, cosmetics, animated_creatures, bosses, worldgen), 4 impossible or not built.

Judgment (U): of the 63 plain archetypes about 18 are thin command / message / timer / data-table plugins that a typed behaviour spec could cover (commands family: custom_commands, utility_commands, kits, tpa_spawn, homes, warps, back_rtp; messages family: announcer, chat_format, chat_filter, join_leave, private_messages, books_guides, sign_tools, holograms; timers: afk, playtime_rewards; data: player_heads). That would raise spec-driven coverage from 21% to about 42% of archetypes. The other ~45 (claims, regions, minigames, clans, economy, auctions, machines, mob AI, structure placement, moderation, ranks) need free-form code and recipes, not specs.

Token effect per hit (V sizes, U equivalence): a designer item spec is about 420-800 tokens (`designer-example.json` 1,669 chars); the same item as Java is about 150 lines / 2k tokens (Spawner Wand: 86 + 67 generated lines) PLUS a 3.2k-line runtime that the model never writes. So 70-90% fewer code tokens, no javac errors from that part, and a smaller solution space for thinking. But: the lane adds 2-8k tokens of system prompt, and the only designer-lane builds in production were the worst ones in the sample (the 10-12 Spawner Wand lineage: 29 files, $0.65 plus repairs, replaced the user's plugin). Spec lanes need planner precision first (regression guard, BJ #2) and no measured cost data exists for them (flights record `costUsd: 0`). XL effort; list as a strategic bet, not a quick win.

# BL: Cyrus token-savings plan (2026-10-12)

Owner goal: if a simple mod costs people too many tokens, Cyrus is not worth it. This note finds every place tokens or compute are spent, measures what can be measured, and ranks the ways to cut spend without making mods worse. It extends BJ (token baseline) and BK (learning loop); BJ's levers are listed in the ranking by number but not re-analysed. Companion: `BL-recipe-memory-design.md`.

Labels: **V** = verified in code (cyrus-rc2) or in read-only SELECTs of the production `ModBuild` table / decompiled jars of the 25 stored builds. **U** = estimate or judgment, with the assumption stated. No build was run, nothing was written anywhere except these two files.

**Sample warning (V):** production holds 28 builds, ALL from the owner (1 distinct user), $7.33 total. Nothing here is a forecast for public traffic. The numbers rank where to look and what to measure.

---

## 0. The five findings that matter

1. **Where the money is (V + U).** Code the model writes is only about 25-40% of a build's cost (U). The rest is thinking before the first edit (planning = 51% of wall time, BJ; the owner saw 3.5-4 min on a 700-word spec), one API round trip per file on Sonnet 5, and cold prompt-cache writes. Shrinking prompts, sheets or boilerplate is therefore worth single digits; model choice, effort, turn count and rework are worth tens of percent.
2. **The Saka tier is on Sonnet 5, not 5.5 (V).** All 12 Saka calls in the data resolved to `claude-sonnet-5` (`MB_TIER_SAKA` default). A fresh Saka build: median $0.55 (range $0.22-0.83), 9-10 turns, 450 s. The 0.3 eval measured Sonnet 5.5 at 2-3 requests and 49% cheaper. This is the largest single lever (BJ #1) and needs no code.
3. **The plan screen under-states cost (V).** I ran the real `estimate()` over the 25 successful builds: **20 exceeded the top of the shown range**, 3 were inside, 2 under. Median actual / shown-high: Saka fresh 2.4x, Saka change 2.5x, Katara change 2.1x, Katara fresh 1.0x, Yakko 1.2x. Users are charged actual cost (not capped at the hold), so the plan screen is the biggest "silently more expensive than shown" problem. See section 3.
4. **Owner's pre-made-structures idea: real but modest on tokens (V shares, U savings).** Of the code the model writes, about 26% is scaffoldable boilerplate (section 4), which is 4-10% of a plain build's cost. Its bigger value is removing failure classes (plugin.yml/getCommand mismatch, unsaved data, reload) and feeding recipes. Typed specs that compile to Java (designer lanes) save far more per hit (70-90% of code tokens) but only 18 of 85 archetypes use them today.
5. **Two things that look like savings are traps (V).** `MB_DEDUPE=on` is cross-user (the key has no user id): it would hand one customer another customer's source, which breaks the owner's "never reproduce a user's mod" rule. And "refunds for guard refusals" only release the hold: `cyrus_tok_charge_refused` defaults to true, so a refused or falsely refused request still costs the 5-token floor.

---

## 1. Where the tokens go (measured, 28 builds)

Spend by call kind from `result.ai.calls` (V):

| kind | calls | turns | spend | share | $/turn |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| change | 13 | 221 | $3.24 | 44% | 0.015 |
| generate | 10 | 61 | $2.93 | 40% | 0.048 |
| repair | 7 | 22 | $0.22 | 3% | 0.010 |
| repair-asset | 2 | 5 | $0.22 | 3% | 0.043 |
| guard | 19 | 19 | $0.08 | 1% | 0.004 |
| (builds before AI records) | | | $0.64 | 9% | |

By model resolved: Haiku 4.5 (Katara) 19 guard + 19 gen/change/repair calls; **Sonnet 5** (Saka) 12 calls, $4.00 (55% of spend); Opus 5 (Yakko) 2 calls, $1.09. Fresh median cost by tier: Katara $0.092, Saka $0.55, Yakko $0.55 (n=2). Opus fresh builds (6-7 turns, $0.41 / $0.69) were NOT dearer than Sonnet 5 fresh builds (9-10 turns, $0.22-0.83): Sonnet 5's turn count eats its price advantage.

Cost anatomy of a typical build (U, from the 0.5 efficiency analysis on the eval mods, `cyrus-v6/efficiency/EFFICIENCY.md`, scaled): output tokens 61% (of which 40-77% is thinking depending on model), cache writes 33% (everything generated is written back to the cache at the 1 h TTL price, 2x input), cache reads 6%. On the owner's heavier prompts the thinking share is higher: a 475 s Sonnet 5 build (ChunkDup, 10 turns, $0.82) wrote about 5.6k tokens of Java (decompiled estimate) plus about 1k of yml/json, but at 60-80 tokens/s it generated roughly 30k+ output tokens, so 60-75% of its output was thinking (U; the service records the exact split in `turnsDetail` on VM 88001, unreadable to me; `CYRUS_LEARNING=1` mirrors it into the portal).

| **base system prompt** | **~10,050** | every build, plus the CLI's tool definitions (U ~2-3k) |
| texture 916, sound 1,561, datapack 2,531, worldgen 1,922, design 2,078, gameplay 1,801, boss 1,892, hud 844, motion 1,491, creature 1,271, item states 1,207, config 653 | up to +18,200 | only when that lane is planned; all lanes together = 28,216 |
| sound library catalog (read into context, `sound-catalog.txt` 22.8 KB) | ~5,700 | sound-library builds |

Cold-prefix cost (U, depends on cache warmth): base 12.5-15k tokens written at the 1 h price = Sonnet $0.05-0.06, Opus $0.13-0.15, Haiku $0.025-0.03; with all lanes 28k = Sonnet $0.11, Opus $0.28. On a $0.09 Katara build or a $0.2 simple Saka build that is 20-50% of the bill when the cache is cold. The guard calls show the warm/cold swing: first-of-day $0.015, warm $0.001. At one user and gaps over an hour between builds, most builds are cold. **Measure first** (section 9): the first turn's `cacheRead` vs `cacheWrite` in `turnsDetail` answers it.

### Silently paid by the user (flag these)

1. **Cold-cache prefix writes and thinking** (rows 9-10): the biggest terms, not visible, not in the estimate.
2. **Repairs and asset repairs on a SUCCESSFUL build** (rows 6-8): fully charged (the failure-credit rule `cyrus_tok_free_failures=3` per 7 days applies to FAILED builds only; over the limit failures are charged in full). The 10-12 Spawner-Wand build spent 33% of its $0.65 on two asset-repair rounds.
3. **Escalation** (row 7): a Katara build can be finished by Sonnet or Opus without telling the user.
4. **The guard** (row 2): charged even when it refuses, including false refusals (the 10-12 06:52 ChunkMirror refusal charged 5 tokens, 215 returned). `cyrus_tok_charge_refused` is a Setting.
5. **Charge is not capped at the hold** (`settleCharge` charges full `costUsd`; the ledger only caps at the balance). With estimates 2.4x low, most builds end "over held". The UI shows it, but the user never agreed to it.
6. **Rework** (BJ: 23% of spend re-requested within 30 min), a share of which is the product's fault (planner turned "mob spawner" into a Spawner Wand and replaced the plugin).
7. **Per-build worst case**: `MB_BUILD_BUDGET_USD=4` and `MB_CALL_BUDGET_USD=2.5` default; the largest observed build is $0.83. A runaway loop could charge 2,000 tokens (40% of a daily cap of 5,000) before it stops.

Not charged to users: planner, coach, Test Flight, javac/scan compute, learning jobs, evals.

---

## 3. Plan screen: honesty about "estimated tokens"

Today (V): `estimate()` = 3 buckets x model `costFactor` (katara 0.5, saka 1, yakko 2.5) x lane weights; anchored on Phase 0 Sonnet 5 / small eval prompts. Real data (shown range = `estimate()` for the stored text, no lane weight):

| group | n | actual median | actual range | shown high (median) | actual / high |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Katara fresh | 6 | $0.092 (46 tok) | 0.038-0.146 | $0.09 | 1.0x |
| Katara change | 7 | $0.159 (80 tok) | 0.082-0.265 | $0.07 | 2.1x |
| Saka fresh (Sonnet 5) | 4 | $0.55 (275 tok) | 0.217-0.825 | $0.18 | 2.4x |
| Saka change (Sonnet 5) | 6 | $0.435 (218 tok) | 0.055-0.648 | $0.14 | 2.5x |
| Yakko fresh | 2 | $0.547 (274 tok) | 0.407-0.688 | $0.45 | 1.2x |

(tokens at 500 per USD.) Also: a change is not 0.8x a fresh build for Katara (1.7x measured; Haiku explores more), but is for Saka (0.8x).

What honest looks like:
- Show **typical and likely-maximum**, from measured medians and p90 by (tier x fresh/change x lane set), with the sample size behind them when small. Until a cell has n >= 8 builds, show the prior but widen it by the measured correction above and say "early estimate". `Setting cyrus_est_table` (new) so it can be corrected without a deploy.
- State the rule in plain words: "You pay what the build actually uses. We hold up to X; the rest is returned." If the owner wants a hard promise, cap the charge at the hold (Nxeon absorbs the overshoot) until estimates are calibrated: owner decision.
- Say what changes the number: tier, edit vs new, each asset lane (lane weights are guesses, 0.05-0.45), sound library, reference images.
- A **recipe hit** (BL-recipe-memory-design) changes the estimate only by a *measured* effect: `typical x recipeEffect[archetype]` where recipeEffect is the median cost ratio from A/B builds, shown only with n >= 8; before that show a badge ("tested pattern: usually fewer fixes") and no discount. Never show a lower number we have not measured.
- A **starter-bank hit** (ready-made build of a template chip, section 5 L4) is a different line item: "Ready-made, instant, ~5 tokens", exact because there is no model call.
- During the build, the live meter exists (V); add a soft stop at 100% of the hold ("This one is bigger than expected: continue / stop with what you have") so the user, not the service budget, decides.

---

## 4. Owner's idea: pre-made structures (measured)

### 4.1 How much of a real build is boilerplate (V shares, U savings)

Method: decompiled (Vineflower) the 25 stored jars, kept only classes the MODEL wrote (excluded the injected `nxperf/` watchdog, 1,009 lines per build, and compiled `designer/`, `abilities/`, `items/`), classified every line by method role. 15 builds, 55 files, 5,840 lines, about 56k tokens (chars/3.5). Our 65 golden plugins (hand-authored reference source, 4,213 lines) for comparison.

| category | real builds (chars) | golden (chars) | scaffold-addressable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| imports + package | 12.8% | 23.4% | yes: API imports can be resolved by the service (autofix already knows the unique FQN); JDK ones stay |
| lifecycle (onEnable/onDisable) | 5.3% | 7.5% | mostly (registration, timers, flush) |
| config loader / clamp / reload | 4.3% | 0 | yes (typed `Cfg` + generated config.yml) |
| persistence (YAML load/save) | 2.6% | 0.8% | yes (`Store`) |
| command dispatch skeleton (onCommand/onTabComplete) | 11.4% | 28.9% | about half: sender/perm/args/usage checks |
| fields, structure, annotations, small helpers | 7.9% | 11.5% | partly |
| **event handlers** | 13.4% | 12.4% | no (skeleton line only) |
| **unique logic** | 41.2% | 15.4% | no |

Realistic saving: imports -80% (10.2 pts), lifecycle -70% (3.7), config -70% plus config-backed fields (5), persistence -70% (1.8), commands -55% (6.3), rest -30% (1.2) = **about 26% of code tokens** (range 20-30%).

Code is 15-40% of a build's cost (ChunkDup 15%, eval-size mods up to 41%; U), so a scaffold saves **4-10% of a fresh plain build** (U). Extra, smaller wins from the same family: derive `plugin.yml` from registered commands (median 576 chars = 170 tokens, V from the jars), `modbuilder.json` commands/permissions/config lists (duplicate of yml; ~200-500 tokens), and `config.yml` vs Config Studio's `schema.json` (both written; schema is the source) = 1-3%.

Where a scaffold also pays: it deletes failure classes the repair loop pays for today (getCommand without a yml entry, no flush in onDisable, no reload, unbounded queue), and is the host for recipes. Same injection mechanism as NxPerf (V: `perf.js inject`, 790 + 219 lines placed before every javac), so there is precedent and a safe pattern.

Verdict: build it, but behind recipes and effort routing in the order (it is an L-size item for single-digit percent). Do not expect it to fix the thinking cost.

### 4.2 Spec-driven archetypes (designer lanes and datapack lanes)

`lib/cyrus/adapters/minecraft-coverage.json`, 85 archetypes (V counts): 63 are "plain plugin / plugin" (54 have a golden), 18 are driven by a typed lane (menus_gui, bossbar_titles, hud_glyphs, sidebar, custom_music, advancements, armor_sets, custom_enchantments, custom_food, custom_weapons, loot, recipes, retexture_vanilla, custom_blocks, cosmetics, animated_creatures, bosses, worldgen), 4 impossible or not built.

Judgment (U): of the 63 plain archetypes about 18 are thin command / message / timer / data-table plugins that a typed behaviour spec could cover (commands family: custom_commands, utility_commands, kits, tpa_spawn, homes, warps, back_rtp; messages family: announcer, chat_format, chat_filter, join_leave, private_messages, books_guides, sign_tools, holograms; timers: afk, playtime_rewards; data: player_heads). That would raise spec-driven coverage from 21% to about 42% of archetypes. The other ~45 (claims, regions, minigames, clans, economy, auctions, machines, mob AI, structure placement, moderation, ranks) need free-form code and recipes, not specs.

Token effect per hit (V sizes, U equivalence): a designer item spec is about 420-800 tokens (`designer-example.json` 1,669 chars); the same item as Java is about 150 lines / 2k tokens (Spawner Wand: 86 + 67 generated lines) PLUS a 3.2k-line runtime that the model never writes. So 70-90% fewer code tokens, no javac errors from that part, and a smaller solution space for thinking. But: the lane adds 2-8k tokens of system prompt, and the only designer-lane builds in production were the worst ones in the sample (the 10-12 Spawner Wand lineage: 29 files, $0.65 plus repairs, replaced the user's plugin). Spec lanes need planner precision first (regression guard, BJ #2) and no measured cost data exists for them (flights record `costUsd: 0`). XL effort; list as a strategic bet, not a quick win.

Measurable now with no spend: spend/turn/rework tables (BJ), estimate error (section 3), boilerplate share (section 4.1), system prompt sizes (section 1), unit prices.

## 9. Legal / privacy

- Recipes and NxKit are authored by Nxeon from our own work: BF technique ids, our golden plugins, failure rules, javap-verified Paper API facts, NxPerf. Each recipe carries provenance and passes a similarity gate against the private reference corpus and every stored user build (n-gram overlap must be ~0). Nothing is taken from a user's mod, an imported mod, or the Modrinth reference corpus (BA: private analysis only).
- Only anonymized outcome data is learned from by default (BK export: counts, lane, tier, model, effort, result, fix ids; no text, names, ids, code). Archetype ids are derived from the guard/planner output, not stored text.

One user, 28 builds; no token counts in `ModBuild`; no designer-lane cost data; no public hit rates; thinking share inferred from time and cost; the CLI's default effort and tool-definition size are U; the build VM's current env is unreadable (assume defaults).

# BL: Recipe memory ("learned paths") design (2026-10-12)

Short design. Context: `BL-token-savings-plan.md` (lever L2, backlog B6/B7), `BK-learning-loop.md` (signals, anonymized export, mining), `BF-mc-technique-catalogue.md` (seed material). V = verified in code/data, U = estimate.

## 1. What it is, in one paragraph

A **recipe** is a small, verified, generic implementation pattern for one mechanic (for example "per-player home store with permission-based limit and safe async teleport"), written by us. At plan time Cyrus picks the matching recipe with a cheap lookup and injects only that recipe into the build's first user turn. A **path memory** table records, per archetype, which lane / tier / effort / recipe actually worked and what it cost, learned from anonymized outcomes, and feeds the plan-screen estimate and the router. Neither one ever contains or is derived from a user's code, an imported mod, or the Modrinth reference corpus.

## 2. Recipe schema (JSON next to the build service, like `rules/failure-rules.json`)

```
services/modbuilder/recipes/<id>.json
{
  "id": "homes-store",
  "version": 3,                       // part of knowledgeVersion() and the dedupe key
  "archetypes": ["homes", "warps"],   // ids from lib/cyrus/adapters/minecraft-coverage.json
  "lanes": ["plugin", "config"],
  "mcVersions": ["1.21.1","1.21.4","1.21.8","1.21.11"],
  "title": "...", "summary": "<= 3 sentences, what the mechanic is",
  "pattern": "<= 600 tokens of prose + at most 40 lines of skeleton, only for the tricky parts",
  "configSchema": [{key, type, default, min, max, why}],   // the keys a mod of this kind should expose
  "paperFacts": ["World#getChunkAtAsync", "Entity#teleportAsync"],  // javap-checked per version
  "pitfalls": [{"ruleId": "ondisable-sync-save", "note": "..."}],   // links to failure-rules.json + BF gotchas
  "boundedWork": "<how NxPerf budgets apply, or 'none'>",
  "tests": "golden/plugins/mc-homes/golden.json",                     // RCON expectations, already exist for 54 archetypes
  "provenance": {"author": "nxeon", "sources": ["BF:plg-safe-teleport-async","golden:mc-homes","rule:ondisable-sync-save"],
                 "noUserCode": true, "noReferenceCorpusCode": true, "reviewedBy": "...", "reviewedAt": "2026-10-.."},
  "stats": {"n": 0, "withRecipe": {...}, "without": {...}},          // filled by the eval, not by hand
  "status": "draft|verified|retired"
}
```

Seed set (all ours): the 33 BF `plugin` techniques with `gotchas` and effort S (safe teleport, teleport warmup/cooldown, config snapshot reload, chest-GUI anti-dupe, ondisable sync save, async chat renderer, playermove filter, hologram text display, per-player FX with reconcile), the bounded-work pattern from NxPerf (perf rule 10), the 54 golden plugins that already map to archetypes (V: 54 of the 63 plain archetypes have a golden), and the 33 failure rules. A recipe is the *explanation + skeleton* of a golden, not a copy of any third-party plugin. Start with 8-12; add by demand from the mining job.

## 3. Selection at plan time (no extra model call)

1. **Free:** the existing intake guard (Haiku, 1 turn, already run on every build, replaces the classifier, V `route.js`) also returns up to 2 archetype ids from the closed list of 85 (about +10 output tokens). Prompt change in `GUARD_PROMPT`/`parseGuard`; unknown ids are dropped.
2. **Fallback / cross-check:** a deterministic scorer over the same 85 rows (label, category, technique words, template tags; there is already a keyword rule set in `lib/cyrus/planner/rules.ts` and a trigram helper `lib/cyrus/prompt-trigrams.ts`). If the guard's id and the scorer agree, confidence high; if only one fires, inject only when the recipe `status` is verified and the match score passes a threshold; otherwise inject nothing. A wrong recipe is worse than none.
3. **Never** inject for: change builds without a mapped archetype, imported mods, refused requests. For a change build, use the base build's recorded recipe id (anonymous metadata we store ourselves), not a fresh match.
4. Result is recorded on the build (`recipeId`, `recipeVersion`, `matchSource`) so the cost effect is measurable.

## 4. Injection (cache-safe, small)

Goes into the first user turn next to `planBlock()` (V: `prompts.js`), NOT the system prompt, so the cached base prefix stays byte-identical:

```
TESTED PATTERN for this kind of mod (follow it unless the request needs something else): <title>
<pattern prose + skeleton> / Settings to expose: ... / Known pitfalls: ...
```

Cost model (U): 600-900 tokens injected = about $0.005-0.008 on Sonnet (one cache write plus ~9 reads); it pays for itself if it removes 700 output tokens of design thinking or one repair turn ($0.010-0.04). Budget cap: 900 tokens per recipe, one recipe per build (two only if they share no pitfalls).

## 5. Path memory (archetype -> best path -> expected cost)

Table built weekly by the learning job (B7), from `BuildSignals` (rework, regression, outcome, cost, turns, effort, model, recipe id, repairs, autofix ids, failure-rule ids):

```
key: (archetypeSet, laneSet, tier, fresh|change)
value: { n, successRate, keptRate, costUsd {p25,p50,p90}, turns p50, repairs p50,
         bestEffort, bestRecipeId, recipeEffect {ratio, ci, n}, lastUpdated }
```

Rules: a cell is shown or used only with n >= 8 (shrink toward the prior `BASE` table below that); "best" = highest keptRate among options with n >= 5, ties by lower p50 cost; a path with one rework in the last 5 is demoted. Used for: (a) plan-screen estimate (typical / up to), (b) default effort and tier suggestion for that archetype (suggestion only, the customer still picks the tier), (c) recipe A/B bookkeeping (`recipeEffect`), (d) the admin Learning tab. It changes nothing automatically: new defaults ship as engine releases through `release-manifest.ts` with an eval gate (BK).

## 6. Learning from outcomes (and what is never learned)

Learned (anonymized, default on, no request text): archetype ids, lanes, tier, model, effort, recipe id, turns, cost, success / kept / rework / regression flags, repair count, **normalized failure signatures** (javac error class plus the Paper API symbol only when it appears in the version's API index; rule ids; autofix ids), and which repair resolved which signature.
Mined into **candidates** (never auto-applied, same as BK): `recipe-pitfall` (signature X recurred in 3+ builds of archetype A without a rule -> propose a pitfall line or failure rule), `path-stat` (a lane/effort combination beats the default), `recipe-gap` (archetype with no recipe and p50 cost above its tier's median -> author one).
Never learned: any user text, class or command names, config contents, code, imported mods, Modrinth corpus code. Recipes are authored and reviewed by us from our own goldens, BF technique ids and javap facts; the mining job only changes *which* of our recipes is chosen and *which pitfall we add*, never the content from a user's work. Template sharing of a user's mod is separate and opt-in (D-60 / D-61 wording).

## 7. Gates before any recipe ships

1. `tools/recipes/lint.ts`: schema, provenance present, every `paperFacts` symbol exists in all listed version jars (javap, as `gen-sheets.py` does), every `pitfalls.ruleId` exists.
2. **Similarity gate:** 8-gram shingle overlap of pattern + skeleton against (a) the private reference corpus index (`/tank/cyrus-library-staging/_reference-mods`, private, offline only) and (b) every stored user build source: must be about 0; a hit blocks the recipe.
3. Golden test: the linked `golden.json` flies green on all four versions.
4. Eval: 2 runs of the archetype's coverage prompts with and without the recipe (about $0.3 per archetype per run on Sonnet 5.5). Ship only if success and first-try are not lower, runtime checks pass, and cost per success is lower or equal (record `recipeEffect`).
5. Rollback: flag `CYRUS_RECIPES` / `MB_RECIPES` off = prompt byte-identical to today (tested).

## 8. Plan-screen implications

- Estimate = path-memory cell (typical / likely max, sample size) x measured `recipeEffect` only when n >= 8; otherwise the plain number plus a badge "tested pattern: usually fewer fixes", no discount. After Saka -> 5.5 and effort routing the cells reset, so `stats` must record the engine release.
- A recipe is a chip the user can see and turn off ("Using the tested Homes pattern"), because it can change the result's shape; off = free-form build and the estimate reverts.
- Identical template-chip prompts can offer the **starter bank** line instead (instant, about 5 tokens), which is the zero-model end of the same idea.

## 9. Rollout

B6 seed 8 recipes + guard archetype ids + injection behind flags (owner/preview accounts first); B1/B7 capture and path memory run in parallel (read-only); eval per recipe; widen to the 54 goldens by mined demand; later NxKit (backlog B9) so recipes call tested helpers instead of carrying skeletons. Expected effect (U): 15-35% per hit build, hit rate 35-55% of plain builds, so 5-19% of spend; the owner's own 13 root prompts would have hit a recipe 3-6 times.

Both files are written. Nothing else was touched: no builds run, no production writes, VM 88001 untouched. Production data is 28 builds from one user (the owner), $7.33 total. Savings below are estimates unless marked measured.

**Top 8 levers, in rank order:**
1. **Saka on Sonnet 5.5.** Measured: Saka still runs Sonnet 5, at 9-10 turns per build against 2-3 on 5.5. About 16-26% of total spend, with no code.
2. **Change-build regression guard.** About 8-16% of spend (from BJ).
3. **Effort routing.** Pick one thinking-effort level per build from the guard's simple/standard/complex rating. About 6-16% of spend; needs an A/B eval.
4. **Calibrated plan-screen estimates.** No savings, but trust. Measured: 20 of 25 builds exceeded the top of the shown range (Saka ran 2.4x over).
5. **Starter bank.** Build the template chips ourselves once and serve them instantly with no model call. Estimated 3-10% of spend; hit rate unknown.
6. **Recipe memory.** Estimated 5-19% of spend; needs an eval.
7. **Change-build hygiene.** Stop the model reading generated NxPerf/designer files on change builds. About 2-6%.
8. **Pre-made structures (NxKit scaffold).** Boilerplate is measured at about 26% of code tokens, but code is only 25-40% of a build's cost, so only 4-10% per plain build. Typed-spec lanes save more per hit but are an XL strategic bet.

**What users pay for without seeing it:**
- Thinking and cold prompt-cache writes.
- Repairs and escalation on builds that succeed.
- The guard's 5-token floor, even on false refusals; `cyrus_tok_charge_refused` defaults to true.
- Charges are not capped at the hold.

**Trap:** `MB_DEDUPE=on` is cross-user and would serve one customer another's source.
